# Graph `example_graph`

## When to use

Use it for questions about items and their condition and for taking items out of service.

## Is it available here?

If you have not yet in this session: `graph start --json` (it refreshes stale skills, lists the graphs and what your token may use of each, and how to search them).

Load the `graph-cli` skill as well before your first `graph` command: it has every command with its options, the change sets of `graph apply` and the error codes. The rules of working with `graph` below hold from the first call, with or without it.

Use this skill only if an item named `example_graph` is listed (title: Example graph) by `graph start` or `graph graphs --json`. Pass `--graph example_graph` to every command, as the examples here do, so they work in every directory; a project whose pointer makes `example_graph` the default may leave it out.

Text values are written in the graph language `en`.

Working with `graph`:

- Run each call as a plain command that starts with `graph` and passes `--json`: no `cd`, variables, loops, pipes or heredocs, which a restricted harness refuses. If a call is refused, run it again in that form before you give up.
- Read the answer: `ok`, then `data`; on failure `error.hint` is the command to run next. Never cut an answer short; ask for less: `--fields <attr>,<attr>` on `find`, `get` and `neighbors`, or `graph query` with `RETURN` of just the columns you need (`graph describe schema --compact --json` lists the patterns).
- For what is known about one entity, `graph view <id> --json` answers in one call (key fields, relations with counts, files, what applies next): use it before walking edges with `get` and `neighbors`.
- Never guess an option, type, field, relation or state: `graph <command> --help` lists the options, `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json` the fields, states and relations.
- For a question, run a named function when one fits (`graph run <function> --param <name>=<value>`); write a `graph query` only when none does. An empty value in a function's answer means nothing is recorded: say so instead of searching further.
- For a change, run a named action when one fits (`graph do <action> --param <name>=<value> --dry-run`, read what it will change, then run it without `--dry-run`). Otherwise preview `create`, `apply`, `transition`, `supersede` and `retract` with `--dry-run`, then run them without; one `update`, `link` or `unlink` may run directly. Say why in `--reason` (in English, whatever language the values are in), and pass `--expect <rev>` when the write depends on what you read. A change set for `graph apply` goes into a file in the working directory.
- Read `data.findings` of every write and tell the user about each warning.

## Subject areas

| Module | Prefix | What it holds | Types | Links to other modules |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `inventory` | `inv` | Physical items, where they are stored and how they are grouped. | 1 | none |

Built-in modules, shared by every graph: `core`.

- Before you work in a module, read it: `graph describe module <module> --graph example_graph` lists its types, its relations, its links to and from other modules (with the other module named) and its rules. Read its text; `--json` is more than twice the size.
- To find a term whose module you do not know: `graph describe search <text> --graph example_graph --json` (types, relations, fields, enum values and states).
- For the fields, states and relations of one type: `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json`.
- The functions and actions of a module are listed by the same command, not here: `graph describe module <module> --graph example_graph`.

## Functions

Named functions: for a question use one before you write a query: `graph run <function> --param <name>=<value> --graph example_graph --json`.

More: `graph describe functions --module <module> --graph example_graph`; find one: `graph describe search <text> --kind function --graph example_graph --json`; columns and use: `graph describe function <function> --graph example_graph`.

## Changes

Named actions: for a change use one before you write with the primitives. Dry run first: `graph do <action> --param <name>=<value> --graph example_graph --dry-run`, read what it will change, then run it without `--dry-run`.

More: `graph describe actions --module <module> --graph example_graph`; find one: `graph describe search <text> --kind action --graph example_graph --json`; preconditions and use: `graph describe action <action> --graph example_graph`. For an entity you already have, `graph get <id> --affordances --graph example_graph` lists the actions that fit it, whether each applies and what blocks it.

## Names and ids

- Aliases: `inv:Item` `ITEM-0001`. The number is zero-padded to 4 digits (`ITEM-0001`, never `ITEM-1`) and grows past 9999. A full id works everywhere; on the command line 8 or more trailing hex digits of it work too.
- No type of this graph has names (label roles), so `graph lookup` finds nothing; use `graph find --graph example_graph`.
- `graph search <value> --graph example_graph --json` searches names and every text field, forgiving case, accents, typos and parts of words. Its results are suggestions: read one with `graph get` before you use it.

## Model

Every type with all its fields, lifecycles, relations and rules: [references/model.md](references/model.md). The live source, which wins when they differ: `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json`.
